statement: Gold is an inflation hedge: it rises when inflation rises.
rationale: As fiat purchasing power erodes, a fixed-supply real asset should hold value. Strongly true in the 1970s Great Inflation.

statement: Gold is a crisis hedge / safe haven during financial and geopolitical stress.
rationale: Gold has no counterparty risk, so it is sought in crises. True for 2008 (eventually), 2020, and the 2022 reserve freeze.

statement: Gold is driven by real interest rates: it falls when real rates rise and rises when they fall.
rationale: Gold pays no yield, so its opportunity cost is the real rate. This explains the 1980-2000 bear, the 2013 taper crash, and the 2020 surge better than inflation alone.

statement: Gold is inversely related to the US dollar: a strong dollar pressures gold.
rationale: Gold is priced in dollars, so a stronger dollar mechanically lowers the gold price and reflects tighter US conditions.

statement: Official-sector (central bank) demand and policy can drive gold independently of inflation or real rates.
rationale: Government revaluation (1934), defense of pegs, and reserve accumulation (2022-2024) show that official flows move gold via demand and valuation effects, not just macro factors.

statement: In 2022 US inflation hit 40-year highs yet gold ended roughly flat, because the Fed raised real rates aggressively.
explanation: Inflation alone does not lift gold when real rates rise sharply; the real-rate hypothesis dominates.

statement: During the worst of the 2008 crisis gold initially fell as investors sold liquid assets to cover losses.
explanation: In acute deleveraging, gold can drop before its safe-haven role reasserts; the hedge works with a lag.

statement: In March 2020 gold briefly sold off in the COVID liquidation before rallying to records.
explanation: Same liquidation dynamic as 2008: cash demand first, safe-haven bid second.

statement: In 2023-2026 gold hit records even with positive real rates, contradicting a pure real-rate model.
explanation: Structural central bank demand and de-dollarization overrode the real-rate headwind.

statement: Gold rose to records in 2024-2026 even during periods of dollar strength.
explanation: Official-sector demand decoupled gold from the usual inverse-dollar relationship.

statement: In the 1990s central banks were net sellers, pushing gold to a $250 low.
explanation: Official-sector flows cut both ways: selling in the 1990s depressed gold just as buying lifted it in the 2020s.
